title: QUIC protocol errors and HTTP/2 fallback with Chromium image-heavy pages
body: In our QUIC-enabled development environment, Chromium-based browsers regularly fail to serve images with `net::ERR_QUIC_PROTOCOL_ERROR 200`. After enough failures, the browser refuses to use QUIC with the origin for a while. The best reproducer is to force QUIC for the origin, open a page containing many images, switch to the grid view so larger thumbnails load, and paginate once or twice. Plain HTML and smaller payloads do not trigger it as regularly. We are running a customized HAProxy 2.8-dev build on Linux with an HTTP/3 QUIC listener, `allow-0rtt`, per-thread shards, a 32768-byte buffer, and QUIC developer tracing to a ring.

symptoms_visible: In Chromium-based browsers, images regularly fail with `net::ERR_QUIC_PROTOCOL_ERROR 200` when loaded over HTTP/3 through HAProxy.
After repeated failures, the browser stops using QUIC with the origin for a while.
Forcing QUIC and paging through a grid of larger thumbnails usually reproduces the problem within one or two pages.
N0.label: N0 Chromium QUIC image failures reported

symptoms_visible: The Chromium QUIC protocol errors remain reproducible while the browser stays open.
N1.label: N1 complete QUIC trace captured

symptoms_visible: With the patch that stops sending STOP_SENDING on HTTP/3 unidirectional streams, Chromium still reports QUIC protocol errors.
The corresponding HAProxy request log entries appear at the error level even though the displayed status is 200.
N2_x.label: N2_x STOP_SENDING patch aftermath

symptoms_visible: The same image requests continue to fail while QUIC, qmux, and HTTP/3 tracing are enabled.
N3.label: N3 combined protocol traces captured

symptoms_visible: With the first mux patch, failures become less frequent, changing from roughly one per 30 images to roughly one per 150 images, but some requests stall for 4–10 seconds.
After the stalls and protocol errors, Chromium retries requests and then falls back to HTTP/2.
In one captured sequence, the second page had three stalled requests, the third had ten, and all 32 requests on the fourth page stalled.
N4_x.label: N4_x first RESET_STREAM patch aftermath

symptoms_visible: On the newer master build with the older patch applied, Chromium reports a QUIC handshake failure within the first 11 small-image requests.
N5_x.label: N5_x old patch on newer master aftermath

symptoms_visible: With the refined patch on the newer master build, about 220 requests initially succeed, then some requests stall for about five seconds, and the next page produces QUIC handshake failures.
N6_x.label: N6_x refined experimental patch aftermath

symptoms_visible: A later 2.8-dev build still produces QUIC protocol errors.
With the local proxy reproducer, roughly half of Chromium sessions encounter QUIC trouble: some break entirely, some only lose images, and others work normally.
N7.label: N7 intermittent local reproducer available

symptoms_visible: After installing a build containing the two later RESET_STREAM fixes, my previous development-environment reproducer no longer triggers the QUIC image failures.
I cannot confirm every production case because I do not have detailed browser-error monitoring beyond user complaints.
N_terminal.label: terminal dev reproducer no longer fails

question_patterns: Can you provide an unfiltered ring capture that includes the complete transport-parameter and connection traces around an occurrence?
Could you capture another reproduction without grepping by timestamp and keep the browser open while copying the trace?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I captured the ring without filtering it. There should be two events, one around 09:26–09:27 and another around 09:29. I kept the browser open before copying it, and the file is the raw haring-format data rather than post-haring text filtered with grep.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The complete trace shows that I closed the browser process immediately before every connection ended.
The same two events are present, but my capture begins a few minutes earlier.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c2-c3: the opening trace had been filtered through haring and grep, so the reporter supplied an unfiltered ring capture and clarified that the browser remained open. This is a measurement-only trace collection on the reporter's existing dev system.

solution.intent: Prevent HAProxy from sending STOP_SENDING frames on HTTP/3 control and other unidirectional streams.
solution.concrete_example: Build and deploy the proposed change that suppresses STOP_SENDING on HTTP/3 unidirectional streams, then repeat the image-grid reproduction.

edges.comment: Participant1 messages c1/c4 proposed and pushed the STOP_SENDING change; reporter message c6 tested it on the reporter's dev environment and reproduced the same errors. The red HAProxy-log screenshot is from the reporter's own system.

question_patterns: Can you enable qmux and HTTP/3 developer traces alongside the existing QUIC trace and capture another failure?
Please collect a reproduction with the transport, mux, and HTTP/3 trace sources enabled.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I enabled the requested qmux and h3 developer traces on the same ring sink and captured another occurrence. Here is the resulting trace archive.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Enabling the extra trace sources prevents the problem from occurring across my repeated sessions.
I captured the same failure with the trace sink set to stdout instead of the ring.

edges.comment: Participant1 messages c7-c8 requested qmux and h3 traces; reporter messages c9-c10 enabled them and returned a new archive. The user answer contains only the capture action and result, not the maintainers' interpretation of RESET_STREAM traffic.

question_patterns: After testing this patch, does Chromium still stop using HTTP/3 following the remaining errors?
Can you show what the Chromium network panel does after the stalls and capture the session with full protocol tracing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. The network panel clearly shows the stalls followed by a regression to H2. In the fully traced session, the first page was fine, the second had three requests that stalled for about ten seconds before a QUIC protocol error and retry, the third had ten stalled requests, and all 32 requests on the fourth page stalled.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The patch eliminates all stalls and Chromium continues using HTTP/3 throughout my repeated pagination.
Chromium still falls back to H2, but my longest measured stall is eight seconds instead of ten.

question_patterns: Can you set qmux and h3 verbosity to minimal and capture the full failing session?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I set h3 and qmux to developer level with minimal verbosity, kept QUIC developer tracing enabled, and captured the session from about 14:27 to 14:28.

solution.intent: Avoid sending an unnecessary RESET_STREAM when the QUIC mux shuts down its write side.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the proposed mux-quic patch that avoids resetting a stream during write shutdown and repeat the image-grid test with qmux and h3 traces enabled.

edges.comment: Participant2 messages c14-c18 supplied the first completed mux-quic patch and trace settings. Reporter messages c20 and c24 tested it on the reporter's dev deployment: errors became rarer but were replaced by stalls, retries, and eventual H2 fallback. The patch therefore did not resolve the issue.

solution.intent: Retest the earlier mux reset-suppression patch on the newer master build containing the recent HTTP/3 connection-shutdown changes.
solution.concrete_example: Build the indicated master revision with the earlier mux-quic patch applied and run the same forced-QUIC image workload.

edges.comment: Participant2 messages c26-c29 requested a new test on the repaired master tip. Reporter messages c30-c31 installed option 1 on the reporter's dev system and saw an immediate new handshake-failure symptom, so this exact build-and-patch combination is a falsified attempt.

solution.intent: Replace the earlier patch with the refined experimental stream-shutdown patch that conditionally sends RESET_STREAM instead of an empty STREAM frame with FIN.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the refined experimental patch to the current master build and repeat the forced-QUIC image test.

edges.comment: Participant2 message c26 supplied the refined experimental patch. Reporter message c32 installed option 2 on the same dev environment; it initially handled about 220 requests but then stalled and ended in handshake failures. This variant was also falsified.

solution.intent: Move to a current unpatched 2.8-dev build and provide a locally runnable proxy configuration so maintainers can exercise the intermittent failure without the obsolete experimental patches.
solution.concrete_example: Run a current 2.8-dev build with the shared local proxy configuration, map the local entry point in the hosts file, force QUIC in Chromium, and load the proxied image-heavy page.

edges.comment: Reporter messages c35-c36: the obsolete experimental patch stopped compiling, so the reporter ran a current 2.8-dev revision and published a local proxy configuration. The reporter's own test still showed intermittent protocol errors, so updating alone was not the resolution, although the reproducer became useful evidence.

solution.intent: Use a HAProxy build containing the two later fixes that remove or reduce spurious RESET_STREAM emissions, then verify the previously failing Chromium image workload before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.concrete_example: Update the development deployment to a build containing both later stream-reset fixes, repeat the forced-QUIC grid pagination test across multiple Chromium sessions, and confirm that the previous reproducer no longer fails.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied protocol traces, patch outcomes, browser-network observations, and an intermittent reproducer. Maintainers concluded that HAProxy was emitting spurious RESET_STREAM frames and later pushed two fixes for that behavior. The reporter did not independently derive that diagnosis from the trace output.

edges.comment: Participant2 message c43 announced two fixes intended to remove or reduce spurious RESET_STREAM frames. Reporter messages c44-c46 installed them on the reporter's dev environment and confirmed that the previous reproducer no longer worked, while explicitly noting the lack of comprehensive production monitoring. Participant2 c47 then closed the issue; release logistics are not scored.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause as HAProxy emitting spurious or unjustified RESET_STREAM frames in the QUIC/HTTP/3 stream handling path, grounded in the collected QUIC, qmux, and h3 traces and the patch-test outcomes.
Must recommend a build containing both later fixes that remove or reduce those spurious RESET_STREAM emissions, rather than relying on the earlier experimental stream-shutdown patches.
Must not present suppressing STOP_SENDING on HTTP/3 unidirectional streams as the fix; the reporter reproduced the same errors after installing that patch.

Must not present either earlier mux reset patch as resolved: one only reduced error frequency while introducing stalls and HTTP/2 fallback, and the later tested combinations ended in handshake failures.
Must ask the reporter to verify the image-grid workload on a build containing the final fixes before declaring resolution.

Resolution may rely on the reporter's confirmation that the development reproducer stopped failing, but must not claim comprehensive production verification because the reporter lacked detailed browser-error monitoring.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical HAProxy operator and developer-build user; comfortable compiling patched HAProxy revisions, configuring detailed ring traces, reading browser network diagnostics, and constructing a local forced-QUIC reproducer.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative, precise, and informal; quickly tests patches, supplies raw traces and screenshots, distinguishes observations from guesses, and openly reports uncertainty or tooling mistakes.
